Stacey emails to clients

Re. Gold Refining:This is the kind of email I send to explain the process/ drawback of reusing your own metal rather than refining it:

Dear [client],

Congratulations on your engagement\! That’s such wonderful news, and I’m thrilled for you and your fiancé. It would be an honor to create a meaningful engagement ring using your family’s combined jewelry. Repurposing heirlooms is a specialty of mine—it’s not only deeply sentimental but also environmentally friendly and cost-effective compared to sourcing new materials.

**Reusing Gold**  
While I love working with clients’ materials, I wouldn’t recommend reusing the old gold directly for casting. Mixed metals, solder, and wear over time can result in porous or pockmarked castings, especially when setting stones (see image below). Additionally, casting requires more gold than you might think because extra metal is needed to create the button and sprue (the parts of the metal tree connected to the ring during casting; see below).

Instead, I suggest refining your gold to extract its pure value, which can then be applied toward your new ring. Refining ensures a flawless result and eliminates the risk of imperfections in the final piece. You can even include small scraps like earring backs, broken chains, or other trinkets in the refining process to maximize the value.

I recommend Hoover & Strong ([https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining](https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining)), a trusted refiner with transparent practices and a low commission. They’ll even cover the cost of shipping your jewelry to them via FedEx. The settlement value you receive can be applied directly to the cost of your new jewelry, and if the refining value exceeds the final cost, I’ll send you a check for the difference. Of course, you’re welcome to use another refiner if you prefer. My role is simply to connect you to a reputable refiner.

**Designing Your Ring**  
Now for the fun part\! To get started, I’d love it if you could send me two types of images:

1\.     Photos of jewelry styles you love, so I can understand your aesthetic and preferences.  
2\.     Photos of the old family jewelry, so I can get a sense of the gems and materials we’ll be working with.

This will help me visualize what’s possible and spark ideas for your design. I’ll also share some options to explore concepts you may not have considered.

From there, we’ll refine the design together—usually through a couple of revisions—until it feels just right. Once finalized, I can provide a detailed cost estimate based on the design, your finger size, and any complexities.

**Budget**  
If you have a specific budget in mind, let me know, and I can try to reverse-engineer the design to align with it. The final cost will include materials, casting, labor, and stone setting. I don’t charge a separate design fee to begin the process, so we can focus on creating something truly special without pressure.

I hope this overview answers your questions\! Let me know if you’d like to move forward, and feel free to reach out with any additional thoughts or ideas. I’m here to help every step of the way.

Warmly,  
Stacey  
p.s. This is the button and sprue you need for casting—the button and sprue are the metal parts connected to the bottom of the ring.:

Another email re. Gold refining. This pertains to the issue of people wanting to use their own gold for sentimental purposes. They do NOT want to replace the old gold for new gold/ cash because the meaning is literally in the metal:

These emails go from oldest to newest:

|  \*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\* Tell Me A Bit About What You Would Like To Make.: Hi , I'm getting married in December and want to see if my grandmother's gold could be used to make my wedding ring. I've attached photos and a video of the pieces. Could you let me know if this is something you can work with, and what the process would involve? Thanks,   |

\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

Hi [client],

Thank you so much for sending over the videos and photos. They were incredibly helpful\!

First of all, you have some beautiful pieces, and from what I can see, they should all yield a very nice refining return.

One thing I did want to mention is that I wouldn't recommend melting these pieces down directly to create your new wedding rings. Chains and earrings like these are assembled using tiny amounts of solder to join the links and components together. When gold containing solder is melted and cast into a new piece, the solder can contaminate the alloy and often leads to porosity and small pits in the finished casting (I've included an image below as an example of what I mean). That's never something I want to risk in a piece that's meant to last a lifetime.

![][image2]

Instead, I would recommend refining the gold. The refiner extracts the pure gold value from your jewelry and sends a settlement payment, which we can apply directly toward your new rings. It's the best way to ensure the new pieces are structurally sound and beautifully cast. And of course, if your refining return ends up being greater than the final cost of the rings, I'll simply send you a check for the difference.

You can also include little odds and ends that tend to accumulate over the years, like broken chains, single earrings, earring backs, scraps, or any other bits of gold, to maximize the refining value.

The refiner I recommend is **Hoover & Strong**. They're incredibly reputable, transparent, and easy to work with, and they'll even provide a prepaid FedEx shipping label to send your jewelry to them. They have a simple form to fill out, and I'm always happy to help you with that if you'd like. Or, if it's easier, you can simply send the jewelry to me and I'll take care of everything on your behalf.

[https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining](https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining)

You're welcome to ship the pieces either directly to Hoover & Strong or to me. Since I don't take any percentage of the refining value, the result is exactly the same either way.

Now for the fun part\!

At this point, I'd love to get a better sense of what you'd like your new jewelry to look like. If you could send me a few inspiration images of styles you're drawn to, that would be incredibly helpful. I'm a very visual person, and photographs communicate so much more to me than words alone. Once I have a clearer picture of your aesthetic, I can start brainstorming ideas, and we'll shape the design together from there.

If you already have a general budget in mind, feel free to share that as well. It doesn't need to be exact. I often find it's easiest to work backwards from a client's comfort zone and design the very best piece we can within it.

I'm really excited about this project and can't wait to see where we take it\!

Yours,

Stacey

\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

Hi Stacey,

Thank you for the detailed explanation and the photos, that's really helpful.

I want to be clear about something: I'm not doing this to save money. This gold belonged to my late grandmother, and using her actual gold is the reason I wanted to do this in the first place.

So a couple of questions: is melting the pieces directly still an option if I'm okay with the porosity risk you described? And if you'd still advise against it, can you help me understand what refining actually preserves, is it truly her gold that ends up in the new rings, just purified, or is it more that the value gets converted and I'd effectively be starting from new material? That distinction matters a lot to me, and if it's the latter, I may not need a custom piece at all.

Best,

\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

Hi [client],

Can you hear me saying, "*Ahhhh\! NOW I get it\!*" all the way from San Francisco? 😊

Now I completely understand, and I'm so sorry I didn't ask you that question in the first place. I get a lot of inquiries from people who simply want to repurpose old jewelry in the most practical way possible, so my brain immediately went there. I wasn't thinking strategically enough.

Now that I understand that the *meaning is in your grandmother's actual gold*, I'm approaching this in a completely different way.

First of all, I'm actually really glad to hear that you're not especially worried about a little porosity. Once I realized this project is about preserving the physical lineage of your grandmother's jewelry/ history, those little quirks become a beautiful part of your family story. If pits or pores end up in the finished ring because we're honoring the original metal, I think that's a wonderful feature—a small tradeoff rather than a flaw.

So here's how I'd like to approach this.

The first thing I'd like to know is exactly what we're working with. Every gold piece should have a tiny hallmark stamped somewhere on it, often near the clasp on chains. Could you let me know what each piece is stamped (it could be a number or a karat)? My guess from the photos is that they're 14 karat, but I really don't want to assume.

Next, could you weigh everything? A simple kitchen scale that measures in grams is perfectly fine. It won't be quite as accurate as my jewelry scale, but it'll give us a very good starting point.

The reason I ask is because when we cast a ring, we don't just need enough gold for the ring itself. The wax model is attached to what's called a sprue and a button (I've attached a photo below). During casting, all of the molten gold first fills that button and then flows through the sprue into the ring. As you can see, the button itself can actually weigh more than the finished ring.

![][image1]

The nice thing is that none of that gold is lost. After casting, your ring is cut off the sprue and button, finished and polished by hand, and all of the remaining gold is returned to you. It's still your grandmother's gold. I just want to make sure we have enough metal to create the casting in the first place.

If it turns out we don't quite have enough, don't worry. I'll come up with another plan. But before we solve a problem, I'd rather find out whether we even have one.

The third thing I'd love is a few inspiration images of the kind of ring you're envisioning. An image really is worth a thousand words here. If you can send me examples you love, along with your approximate ring size (or even just the width you're imagining), I can start working backwards from the amount of gold you have and figure out what makes the most sense. If we need to conserve metal, perhaps we make the band just a touch narrower or adjust the profile. There are lots of creative ways to solve that puzzle.

Do you happen to know your ring size? If not, no worries at all. I often recommend this ring sizer from Amazon (I’ve attached the link below). I like when we're both working from the same ring sizer because different manufacturers can vary slightly, and this way I know I'll get the fit exactly right.

[https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01CCG6IQY?psc=1\&ref=ppx\_pop\_dt\_b\_product\_details](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01CCG6IQY?psc=1&ref=ppx_pop_dt_b_product_details)

And one very last thing. I'm going to speak with my caster about the chain and bracelet specifically. Those are the two pieces that concern me most because of all the solder joints. I want to see whether he's comfortable casting directly with them. If he isn't, then we'll put our heads together and come up with another solution. One way or another, we'll figure out the best path forward while staying true to what matters most: preserving your grandmother's gold.

Thank you, truly, for steering me in the right direction. Knowing the story behind this project changes everything for me. It makes it so much more meaningful, and I'm genuinely excited to help you create something that carries her forward every single day.

Yours,

Stacey

Hi [client],

Thank you so much for reaching out—I’m so glad you did. You picked a ring that’s very close to my heart; that branch design has always been one of my personal favorites.

I’d absolutely love to help you reuse your gold and diamonds to create a platinum version of it. Here’s how I begin a project like this:

1\. Ring size  
The first thing I’ll need is your ring size. That helps me determine how much platinum will be required for the new design.

2\. The diamonds you’d like to use  
It would be helpful to know how many diamonds you have and their approximate sizes. Once I have that, I can lay out the design to suit your stones perfectly.

3\. Refining your gold jewelry  
Even though the final piece will be cast in platinum, your existing gold/ other jewelry should definitely be used toward the project. The best approach is to refine it. Refining extracts its pure value, which you can then apply toward the cost of your new platinum ring. You can include anything from broken chains to single earrings to maximize what you get back.

I recommend Hoover & Strong ([https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining](https://www.hooverandstrong.com/landing/Refining)), a trusted refiner with transparent practices and a low commission. They’ll even cover the cost of shipping your jewelry to them via FedEx.  
Of course, you’re welcome to use any refiner you choose; my role is simply to connect you with a reputable option.

If your gold jewelry contains diamonds, Hoover & Strong can safely remove them and return the stones either directly to you or to me, whichever you prefer.

If your jewelry contains colored gems or pearls you want to save, please send those pieces to me first. Hoover & Strong uses a chemical process that’s ideal for diamonds but destructive to other stones. Many clients are happy to let old beads or non-valuable stones be destroyed in refining, but if there’s something you want saved, I’m I can remove it safely before the gold is refined.

4\. Budget  
Once I know your ring size, the stones you’d like to use, and the value of the metal available for refining, I can put together a ballpark estimate.

If you'd like to move forward, feel free to send photos of the diamonds or any jewelry you plan to repurpose. That will help me begin ruminating on the possibilities.

I hope this answers your question, but if I missed anything, please let me know—I’m happy to clarify\!

Yours,  
Stacey

Hi [client],

I’m so glad this all sounds good to you — I’m really excited to get started\!

There are two ways we can go about it:

Option 1 is to send everything to me first. I can have my gem setter safely remove any pearls and colored stones (like the jade and those darker ones — maybe onyx? Hard to tell from the photo), and then I’ll send the remaining gold on to Hoover & Strong for refining. This option is best if you’d like to keep as many stones as possible, since the chemical process Hoover & Strong uses to extract diamonds can damage more delicate stones. That said, there’s a bit of labor cost associated with removing stones here on my end — but we’ll avoid splitting up your return into two shipments, which helps maximize the metal weight in a single batch (the more you refine at once, the better your payout).

Option 2 is simpler: send everything directly to Hoover & Strong. They'll chemically remove any diamonds and melt down all the metal — and send the diamonds back to you or to me. This is a great option if you're not especially attached to saving every single stone. Many clients go this route when they’re not planning to reuse the colored stones and are ready to part with them. Just don’t include pearls — the chemical process will destroy them\! If your pearl necklace has a gold clasp, just snip it off with scissors and pop the pearls in the mail to me separately.

Whichever route you choose, Hoover & Strong offers clear documentation and full transparency — you’ll get a settlement value for the refined metal, which I’ll apply directly toward the cost of making your new pieces. I don’t take a percentage or cut; this is just your credit to use. Depending on what we end up making, you might owe a bit more, or we might land under — in which case I’ll send you a check for the difference.

And if you have any other old gold or platinum lying around that you're ready to let go of — even tiny things like earring backs, broken bits of chain, etc. — I definitely recommend including them in the refining batch. It’s better for the environment *and* it boosts your payout for the new jewelry.

Let me know which direction you’d like to take, and I can walk you through the next step\!

Warmly,  
Stacey

Hi [client],

I hope you're having a wonderful day\! Thanks for sending over those photos—they're extremely helpful, and I've also saved the inspiration photo of the ring you love to our thread.

Here’s our plan for creating your new piece:

1. **Refinement**: We can refine all your jewelry, whether it's 10k, 14k, white or yellow gold. This process includes carefully removing your old stones, which I'll then assess to select the perfect ones for your new ring.  
2. **Designing Your Ring**:  
   * **Width**: Let’s decide the ideal width for your ring. A good method is to cut strips of paper in various widths, wrap them around your finger, and see which one looks best.  
   * **Thickness**: For comfort and durability, I recommend a thickness of 2-2.5mm, especially for chunky rings.  
   * **Profile**: Do you prefer a half-round profile like your inspiration ring, or something different? Let me know if you’d like it to taper or be uniform all around. I included an image below so you know what I mean by “ring profile.”  
   * **Texture Options**:  
     * **Smooth Finish**: We can opt for a smooth matte finish, like in your original inspiration ring.  
     * **Hammered Look**: Alternatively, you can consider a lightly or heavily hammered texture. I'll add the texture towards the end of the process and share photos and  videos with you. This way, you can confirm if it matches your vision or if we need to make adjustments. Below, I've included images of black diamond bands and a diamond heart ring to illustrate just a couple different textures. Rest assured, we'll fine-tune the details to ensure your ring turns out exactly as you envisioned.  
3. **Ring Size**: Knowing your ring size is crucial. If you're unsure, I can recommend an inexpensive ring sizer from Amazon to ensure accuracy. Alternatively, visiting a local jewelry store for sizing is also a great option.  
4. **Estimate Preparation**: Once I have the dimensions and your ring size, I’ll prepare an estimate for your review.

If you're ready to refine your old jewelry, I’ll assist you with the forms and provide a free FedEx shipping label for secure sending. If possible, could you weigh the jewelry? Even a weight on a kitchen or postal scale if fine. This gives us a starting point, although the refiner will do a precise weighing on receipt.

Please don't hesitate to ask if you have any more questions—I'm here to help every step of the way\!

Warmly, 

Stacey

This is an old email I used to send to potential customer re/ custom rings:  
Dear      ,  
   
Congratulations on taking this next step with —this is wonderful news\!  Custom engagement rings and wedding bands are my specialty; I create one-of-a-kind pieces tailored to each client’s aesthetic, as well as to his or her budget.  I’ve created rings for $100,000, I’ve created rings for $500—other than the choice of materials, I believe you’d have difficulty telling the difference.  I don’t gravitate toward flashy or large diamonds—my paramount interest is in the quality of the design.  
   
To that end, I’d work with you and your partner to design and fabricate a ring that she’d love (or just you, if you would prefer to keep it a secret).  I have many images you can look at for inspiration, and I would also be setting up a digital mood board so you and I can upload images of rings you think she’d like.  Developing the design is a fun, collaborative experience, and I know we’d have no difficulty creating something that she’d adore.  
   
In tandem with the design discovery process, you’d determine a comfortable ballpark budget.  From strategic choices of metals and gems, to savvy diamond or gem options, my job is to work backward from your budget, and to provide creative ways to maximize it.  Because my prices are more in line with wholesale rather than with retail, your budget will go farther, and you’ll have a beautiful, unique custom ring that truly suits you, and not a generic token.  
   
On a more personal note, I’ll add that after years of making custom engagement and wedding rings, I’ve discovered a fair bit—not just about my craft, but about the people for whom I’ve made them.   I’ve learned there’s no correlation between budget and the sentimental value of the ring.  The ring should serve as a talisman to remind you both of the significance of your relationship and the vows you will take; it should not be an expression of your net worth, or your future earning potential.  I urge you to detach those economic connotations from the ring, pick a budget that’s reasonable \[and not punitive\!\] for you, and enjoy the design and fabrication of this gift.   
   
Feel free to ask any questions you may have; my website, www.Lorinczi.com, will also be informative.  I have examples of past work, but my rings are all custom, and dictated solely by what each client wants. I mostly put the unusual pieces on display; if you see nothing that interests you on the site, rest assured your ring design would be determined by you, and not imposed by myself\!  
   
All my best,  
Stacey

Dear [client],  
   
Again, thank you so much for reaching out to me, and for the kind words about my work\!  You had asked about how my process work, so I’ll try to fill you in here-- of course, if there’s anything I’ve neglected to cover, please don’t hesitate to ask.      
   
Custom engagement rings and wedding bands are my specialty; I create one-of-a-kind pieces tailored to each client’s aesthetic, as well as to his or her budget.  I’ve created rings for $100,000, I’ve created rings for $500—other than the choice of materials, I believe you’d have difficulty telling the difference.  My paramount interest is in the quality of the design, not the carat weight of the stones.  I believe that good design should never be hampered by one’s choice of materials or budget size.  
   
To that end, I’d work with you to design and fabricate a ring based on whatever you have in mind; I have many images you can look at for inspiration, and we would also be setting up a digital mood board (most likely on Pinterest) so we can easily upload images of rings that inspire you. The two most pressing concerns new clients tend to have are the opacity of the fabrication process (will it come out just as I imagine?), and the cost. On a more personal note, I’ll add that after years of making custom engagement and wedding rings, I’ve discovered a fair bit—not just about my craft, but about the people for whom I’ve made them. I urge clients to detach economic connotations from the ring, pick a budget that’s reasonable \[and not punitive\!\] for you, and enjoy the design and fabrication of this gift to yourselves.

Dear [client],  
   
Thank you so much for the kind words—I’m new to social media and tend more toward Instagram than TikTok, so I’m glad you found me\!  
   
I’d love to help you create a custom signet ring; that’s right up my alley. To answer your questions, I *do* think it may be worth exploring what the Webb earrings may fetch. Sadly, I haven’t worked personally with resellers, so I don’t have a vendor I could recommend. Still, I think perhaps Circa or The RealReal may be worth contacting for an estimate and a quote on their commission (and, of course, 1st Dibs or eBay). David Webb comes in and out of great popularity, depending on current trends. I appreciate David Webb, but some of their pieces have such a strong aesthetic that they can overpower the wearer.   
   
The pieces I inherited from my mother were similar—directional and exciting, but every time I wore them, I felt like I was wearing a costume. *Totally* not me. Finally, after decades of the pieces languishing in the safe and my turning 50, I decided enough already. If I haven’t worn this stuff in almost 30 years, odds are I never will. Time to make it all into pieces that reflect who *I* am, not a shrine to who my mother was.  
   
This is all a long-winded \[and weirdly personal—my apologies\! My daughter just graduated high school and you've caught me in a reflective mood 🤷‍♀️\] way of saying *yes*, *go for it.* Let’s collaborate on something that reflects your own aesthetic\!  
   
My chief role in this—even before we get to the fun part about my creating a custom piece for you—is trying to get you the greatest return for your gold. With the David Webb earrings and also the Hermes ring, I’d say first submit pictures to Circa, The RealReal, etc., to see if the resale value (minus their commission) would give you a better return than simply refining the metal.  
   
If it turns out that refining is the better option, then I would send everything to my refiner, Hoover & Strong (https://www.hooverandstrong.com/). They adhere to good practices (environmental as well as anti-money laundering, transparency, etc.), and I believe that their commission is quite low.  
   
I’ll attach a copy of one of my customer’s refining settlements so you can see how they go about weighing everything as well as the commission they take, what they charge for stone removal ($50, which they categorized as a "refining fee," $15 to FedEx the removed stones back to me), etc.   
   
The settlement you receive from the refining is deducted from the cost of your new piece. And if, for example, your new custom piece costs *less* than the amount you received from your refining, I’ll send you a check for the difference when I ship you your final piece. Whether you use my refiner or another is not of great import to me, my role is simply to find you a reputable refiner who takes a minimum percentage.   
   
Now on to the more exciting part of the equation: creating a new piece for you. The way it works is you send me images of signet rings that appeal to you, so I get a sense of what you’re after. There are so many different styles and shapes available to us. I really look forward to gaining a better understanding of your aesthetic and the kind of shapes you love, as well as whether or not you want it to be all white metal (we can nail down what specific metal later) or be adorned with diamond(s) or other gemstones, engraving, etc. Pictures are worth more than words at this point, so we’ll really be able to get the ball rolling once I know what you’d like to achieve. And I'll also send you photos to steer you toward options you may not have considered.  
   
Then we can hammer out a final design (usually after a couple of revisions), at which point I’ll be able to estimate final costs. Also, we can discuss doing a locking shank as we hammer out the design. My knuckles have also grown, so I know what you mean. 🤦‍♀️  
   
Finally, once you decide whether or not you’d like first to try selling some of your jewelry intact or want me to just go ahead and refine what you already have, I think what might be most straightforward is to have you send the pieces directly to Hoover & Strong (not to worry if your weights may not be perfectly exact. Hoover & Strong will carefully weigh everything you send them, take a photo of it, and the incoming weight will be listed on your refining settlement).   
   
They also provide pre-paid, insured FedEx labels to make it easier. I do *not* know if their refining settlement terms are as generous with private individuals as they are for wholesale jewelers. More often than not, customers bring me their jewelry directly, so I’ve never had to inquire. If it turns out that you’ll get a higher return if I send in the gold using my wholesale account, then I’ll simply email you a pre-filled refining form with my wholesale account information included. Whatever you prefer.  
   
Anyway, I feel like I’ve been rambling on an absurdly long time. If you have any questions and a simple phone call could be more efficient, please contact me at 415-425-7394 (my time zone is PST). I’ll be in the studio almost all day tomorrow and look forward to touching base with you via phone or email.  
   
In the meantime, I’ll send you some of my favorite signet-style rings I’ve made (just for fun\!).  
   
Have a lovely evening,  
Stacey

> On Tue, Aug 4, 2026 at 10:07 AM stacey lorinczi \<stacey@lorinczi.com\> wrote:

Hi [client],

Thank you so much for reaching out. Your project sounds absolutely wonderful, and I have to say it's always exciting—not to mention incredibly helpful—when clients have such a clear, well-thought-out vision before we begin. It makes my job much easier, and I love collaborating with people who have already spent time dreaming about what they want.

And thank you for asking such thoughtful questions.

The answer is a definite yes to the first two; to the third, re. turquoise inlay, the answer is no.

I regularly work in both 950 platinum/ruthenium and 950 palladium/ruthenium. Personally, I much prefer ruthenium to iridium as an alloy, so we're already on the same page there. I also love working with clients' heirloom stones. To me, that's often what makes a custom piece truly meaningful. Not only is it cost-effective, but there's something really special about carrying family history forward into a new design.

The only hesitation I have is regarding using turquoise.

It's not that I don't appreciate the aesthetic—I absolutely do—but whenever I make a piece of jewelry, especially a wedding ring, my number one priority is longevity. My hope is always that the piece will still be worn and loved fifty or a hundred years from now.

You've already made wonderful material choices in that regard. Platinum is about as durable as it gets, and diamonds are a perfect 10 on the Mohs hardness scale, making them ideal for something that's worn every day.

Turquoise, on the other hand, is only about 5–6 on the Mohs hardness scale, which makes it relatively soft. It's prone to scratching, and because it's naturally porous, it can absorb oils, lotions, soaps, perfumes, and even your skin chemistry over time, gradually changing color. Inlay presents another consideration, since it's typically held in place with an epoxy or adhesive. Modern epoxies can be remarkably durable—and they may very well help protect the turquoise from day-to-day wear—but they're still another material that ages differently than platinum itself.

None of this is to say, "Don't do it." I certainly don't want to discourage you if it's something you've truly fallen in love with. I just think it's important that whoever makes the rings talks through the long-term implications with you so you're making an informed decision. My greatest wish is that your wedding rings still look beautiful decades from now, so I always try to think well beyond the day they're made. 

However, I tend to be fairly rough on my jewelry since I’m a maker, always using my hands and knocking them about–it’s entirely possible I’m being overly cautious. There is so much gorgeous turquoise jewelry out there that’s been around for decades and decades, so please don’t let me dissuade you. It’s a beautiful stone and I think if you have your heart set on it you should go for it\!

Whether or not I'm ultimately the right jeweler for this project, I'm always happy to share my thoughts and help you think through the engineering and material choices. My goal is simply that you end up with rings you'll absolutely love for the rest of your lives, even if I’m not the one to create them for you.

I look forward to hearing from you, and thank you again for thinking of me.

Warmly,

Stacey

Hi\!

Thank you so much for reaching out, and I’m so glad you found my work\! This is absolutely the kind of project I love to take on. Those sound like beautiful diamonds.

Although I work with clients all over the world, it’s honestly so much more fun when I get the chance to work with someone locally here in the Bay Area. If you’d enjoy meeting in person, please do let me know what part of the the Bay you’re in and when might work for you.

In the meantime, I’d absolutely love to see if you have any images of rings you might want to create or that resonate with you aesthetically. For me, the most interesting and enjoyable part of meeting a new client is understanding their inspirations, their personal style, and what they want their jewelry to feel like when they wear it. Some people are drawn to very clean, architectural forms, while others love antique details, organic textures, or more sculptural, artistic pieces. Just as importantly, I love learning about how people actually live with their jewelry. For example, many of my clients work in medicine or science and prefer low-profile bezel settings rather than higher prong settings because they wear gloves every day. Others prioritize stacking, durability, comfort, or creating a piece that feels quietly timeless versus boldly expressive.

There are no right or wrong answers here—I often find that even a handful of saved images can tell me a tremendous amount about someone’s aesthetic instincts and help guide us toward a design that feels deeply personal and uniquely theirs.

I’d also love to see a few photos of your diamonds—it would be wonderful to see them side by side if you’re considering incorporating them into a single piece. Seeing their scale in relation to one another, and especially seeing them placed on your finger, really helps me begin to visualize the possibilities and think about proportion, presence, and how the finished piece might feel when worn.

As for any other jewelry you might be interested in recycling, most definitely—I love getting old gold and platinum back into the supply stream. The refining credit can be applied directly toward the cost of the new piece, and depending on how much material you have, it’s sometimes possible to offset a substantial portion of the project cost, or even cover the cost of the new ring entirely.

If you don’t mind, the easiest way to start the conversation is usually over email, simply because it’s so much easier to look at images and keep track of inspiration. My email is Stacey@Lorinczi.com, and I’d be delighted to take a look at whatever you’d like to send.

I’m really looking forward to seeing your stones and learning more about what you’re imagining\!

Warmly,

Stacey

Great question. I don’t charge a separate design fee for this, since the ring is essentially already designed. The cost for the new ring will be based on how much metal we use, as well as how many stones need to be set.

You can show me the stones you’d like to use, and based on how many there are and their sizes, we’ll determine the best width and height for the ring. Once I know your finger size, the overall dimensions, and how many stones you want to set, I can give you a cost estimate to create the new ring, and you can decide then if you’d like to go ahead and have me make it for you.

The majority of the cost for a ring like this is in the gold and the labor involved in setting the stones. Any estimate I provide will have some flexibility—we can always adjust the width, height, or number of stones to move the cost up or down (as well as the gold karat—14 karat will, of course, cost less than 18 karat, though I can provide estimates for both).

If you have enough gold to refine, it’s possible that the value of the metal you already own could fully offset the cost of the ring. I’ll have a better sense of that once I know how much metal you’d like to refine and how big, wide, or tall you’d like the new ring to be.

Once you email me, I’m also happy to share information for my refiner. You’re welcome to send your jewelry directly to them if you prefer. I don’t take any cut from the refining process—the metal and its value are entirely yours to use however you’d like. :-)

Hi [client], thank you so much for the kind words\! 😌

Most of my customers are actually remote, so yes, I definitely ship. That ring was custom—it was made for a man with a pretty large finger size. Were I to make it for you, I imagine yours would cost less since you would have a smaller ring size.

I generally try to work backwards from my customer’s budget whenever possible, so I can do a rough estimate based on your finger size, what karat gold you’d like, how big the stone would be, etc., and give you a ballpark. Tape the strips of paper around your finger, and play around to see what looks and feels best. Then let me know, and we’ll proceed from there\! 

Oh, yes, and in terms of sizing your finger, I recommend either popping into a local jewelry store to have them size you with a wide ring sizer, or order a ring sizer from Amazon. Just make sure it’s a metal sizer and not a plastic one, in order to get the most accurate gauge. Sound good?

On Recycling a Customer’s Jewelry:

Hi\! Thank you for your question; it’s an excellent one\! Here’s how it works. First, send me pictures of the kind of jewelry you’d like me to create. If I’m a good person to make it, I’ll provide a ballpark budget–or, you can give a budget you’d like to work with, and I’ll work backward from it–and we’ll start finalizing the design. 

At the same time, you’ll gather the jewelry you want to recycle, and I’ll send you instructions for how to package it safely and send you a pre-paid FedEx shipping label so you can send your jewelry to my refiner at no cost.

They will provide a document that includes the total weight of your metal pieces, your payout, etc. (I included an image of what one of their refining settlements looks like, FYI). If your jewelry contains gemstones, they can safely remove them for a small fee (I believe they charge a flat $50). They will send me your stones and I can either include them in your new piece or return them to you when your new piece of jewelry is finished. 

The payout you receive from the refiner is deducted from the cost of the new piece I make you. I do NOT take an extra, hidden percentage of the value of your refining (which is a common practice, sadly). Instead, all the money you receive from your gold refining will be applied in full to offset the cost of your new piece.

If, however, you do not want me to make you a new piece of jewelry, and you simply want to refine your gold and receive a cash payout, I completely understand\! 😊 You may prefer to take the money you receive from refining your old jewelry and put it toward something other than a new piece of jewelry. If that’s the case, I’m not the person for you. You should send it directly to a refiner; many reputable ones are a Google search away. :-)

I hope that helps answer your question, but please don’t hesitate to ask me any questions that spring to mind. Take care, and have a wonderful day\! 😊

How to find your ring size \#1  
18 June 2023|Find your ring size, Jewellery Sizing  
￼  
There are a number of ways to find out your ring size, to help you choose a ring that will be the most comfortable fit.  
Although, I've owned a small adjustable plastic ring sizer for many decades, I don't recommend plastic products, so I have some plastic free alternative options for you.  
Firstly, choose a ring that fits the finger that you would like to know the size of and choose a ring that still comfortable to wear when the weather is warm.

There ways to find out your ring size:  
1\. You can use a ring sizing app \- there's a great one called 'Ring Sizer by Jason Withers' in the iPhone app store (it's also available for Android phones). It is simple to use and instructions are within the app.  
2\. You can follow the guidance in my ring sizing chart on my jewellery sizing guide page. You'll need a ruler to use with the chart.  
3\. You could invest in a quality set of metal ring sizers but this can be expensive, and unless you're a jeweller, you won't have much use for them once you've identified your ring sizes.   
4\. Finally, you could visit a high street jewellers and ask to be measured.

Did you know you need to up-size for wider ring bands?  
If the ring you're interested in purchasing has a band that is wider than 4mm, you'll likely need to choose a larger ring size to be sure of a comfortable fit:  
	•	If the ring band is 4-6mm wide, it's recommended that you add on 1/2 a size \~ e.g. if you measured a ring size M, choose ring size M 1/2  
	•	If the ring band is 7mm wide and over, it's recommended that you add on 1 full size \~ e.g. if you measured a ring size M, choose ring size N  
Taking this approach will account for the wider band and ensure you have a comfortable fit when wearing it.  
I'd be happy to answer any questions you have about ring sizing so please send me a message at [email removed]  

Looking for a US or International to UK ring size comparison chart?  
You can find a UK & International ring size comparison chart on my jewellery sizing guide page.

How to find your ring size \#2  
18 June 2023|Find your ring size, Jewellery Sizing  
￼

There are a few ways to find out your ring size if I can’t size you myself.

1.) Visit a local jewelry store and ask to be measured.  
2.) Buy an inexpensive metal ring sizer on Amazon—I recommend this one, “Mudder Stainless Steel Ring Gauges Finger Sizer Measuring Ring Tool, Size 1-13 with Half Size, 27 Pcs” (for less than $10). Do NOT use a flexible plastic ring measuring tool (they can be inaccurate).   
￼  
3.) You can use a ring sizing app. I recommend 'Ring Sizer by Jason Withers' in the iPhone app store (it's also available for Android phones). It’s simple to use and instructions are within the app. Just make sure to cross-reference your results with one other source to make sure your sizing is as accurate as possible.  
￼

What’s my process?

Thank you so much for the kind words\! You made my day\! 😌

To answer your question about how this works, we’d start the design process by having you send me images of the pieces you have and any images/ descriptions of what new piece you envision. Developing the design is a fun, collaborative experience, and I know we’d have no difficulty creating something you'd adore and want to wear all the time.  
In tandem with the design discovery process, you’d determine a comfortable ballpark budget.  Utilizing strategic choices of metals and gems, my job is to work backward from your budget as much as possible. 

We can re-use gems you already own or get new gems (totally up to you\!). If there’s metal from any of your old jewelry that we can refine (leftovers from the heirlooms or any little bits and bobs of gold jewelry you already own like chains, earring backs, etc.), I can apply the money you receive from refining your old metal to offset the cost of the new piece. I do not take an extra, hidden percentage of the value of your refining, which is a common practice, sadly. Instead, all the money you receive from your gold refining will be applied in full to offset the cost of your new piece.

If it all possible, I find it a bit easier to communicate larger text threads and images through email. My address is stacey@lorinczi.com. Just DM me on Instagram to let me know when you’ve emailed me because for some reason people emails from Instagram often get lost in my junk mail folder—I wouldn’t want you to think I’ve neglected you\! ☺️

I’m looking forward to seeing what you have to work with and helping to create a new piece you love\! 🤗🌺

Warmly,  
Stacey

When re-using old jewelry, is it one-to-one?

Hi\! Thanks so much for reaching out to me—that’s a great question\! Sadly, the process of transforming an old ring into a new ring will require more metal. It isn’t a one-to-one transformation because you need enough metal for the button and the sprue (these are parts of the casting “tree”; I included this picture of a ring after it’s been cast and before cleaning/ polishing. The button and sprue are the metal parts connected to the bottom of the ring).

Also, re-using old gold/ platinum in a new casting can lead to pitted, pockmarked  castings (I attached a picture to show you what I mean). I prefer to refine any jewelry you have and you can take the payout you receive to offset the cost a new ring made properly with clean, recycled metal.

I hope that answers your question, but feel free to reach out to me at Stacey@Lorinczi.com with any other questions. I’d love to see the ring you currently have, and the new one you’re envisioning. 🤗

I usually suggest sending your jewelry to my refiner, Hoover & Strong. They’ll carefully remove the stones, refine the metal, and send you a check for its value. Then they can ship the diamonds straight to me so I can start your new piece.

You’re always welcome to use any refiner you like—I don’t take any percentage of your metal value. I just recommend Hoover & Strong because they cover shipping and make it really easy.

Fresh metal (paired with your stones) always gives the best results. Once you send me a few inspiration photos, we can dream up the design together—whether that’s a necklace, another ring, or something totally new. And if it’s easier, you can also just send everything to me and I’ll handle the refining process for you.

Cost?

Great question\! I don’t charge a separate design fee—just for the finished piece itself, which includes labor, metal, setting costs, and so on. The total really depends on what we’re making, how detailed or complex it is, and how much metal it requires.

The best way to get a sense of cost is to send me a few inspiration images of jewelry you love. From there, I can estimate what it might take to create something similar so we have a ballpark. I’m also happy to work backwards from your budget, adjusting the design so it fits comfortably within your parameters.
